title: The popular version. Removing the pump handle did not end the cholera outbreak.
description:
Removing the pump handle did not end the cholera outbreak. Deaths were already falling. Whitehead's table shows fatal attacks dropping from 142 on 1 September to 14 on 8 September, the day the handle came off.

On or near Broad Street in the first three days, in Soho in 1854. By the end of the outbreak the toll was 420.

John Snow mapped the cases. The deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump. None of the workers at the nearby brewery caught cholera, and they drank a beer allowance instead of the well water.

The man who traced the first case had started as a doubter. Rev. Henry Whitehead believed in bad air until Snow's maps convinced him. He traced the outbreak to an infant at 40 Broad Street.

The authorities still blamed bad air. London's Board of Health ultimately attributed the epidemic to miasma. William Farr only accepted Snow's diagnosis in 1866.

His water test proved nothing. The pattern of the deaths made the case.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak: read. Established that the outbreak hit Soho in late August 1854; that 127 people on or near Broad Street died over three days and 420 by the end; that Snow mapped the cases; that none of the workers in the nearby brewery contracted cholera, because they received a beer allowance and did not drink the well water; that removing the handle is popularly reported as ending the outbreak though it may already have been in rapid decline; and that the London Board of Health ultimately attributed the epidemic to miasma.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Snow: read. Established that Snow observed the epidemic may already have been in rapid decline when the handle was removed, and that William Farr realised the validity of Snow's diagnosis only in 1866.
- https://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/snow/removal.html: read. Established Snow's account of meeting the Board of Guardians of St James's parish on Thursday 7 September with the handle removed the next day; Snow's statement that the attacks had so far diminished before use of the water was stopped; and Rev. Henry Whitehead's 1867 table showing fatal attacks falling from 142 on 1 September to 14 on 8 September, plus his note that the commonly supposed arrest of the outbreak by closing the pump is a mistake.
